weeks.title: God’s Household: Committing to a Church
weeks.theme: The church isn’t a place I go; it is the family I belong to. Commitment is love’s response to God’s household.
group: What was your impression of “church” before? And now?
How does the word “commitment” make you feel?
What is one thing you could do for your church family?
weeks.guide: The first three months after baptism are when new believers most easily drift away. Help them move from “coming to church” to “belonging to church”: attending Sunday worship regularly, getting to know the pastor and a few brothers and sisters, understanding the church’s vision and membership. If they have been hurt or have seen imperfection, help them see the church through God’s eyes: a home of forgiven sinners—imperfect yet precious. You can also introduce the 321 online gatherings so they have a spiritual community every day.
weeks.meet: This week, attend a Sunday service with the person walking with you, then have a meal and talk: what role could I have in this family?
weeks.keyText: So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,

lessons.title: No Longer Strangers
text: So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God,
being built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the chief cornerstone;
in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord;
in whom you also are built together for a habitation of God in the Spirit.
lessons.hear:
Some people attend church for years yet always feel like “guests”: they come, sit, listen and leave without anyone noticing. Paul tells believers: “So then you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints and of the household of God” (Ephesians 2:19).

“Household of God” is a warm identity. What is the biggest difference between a guest and family? Guests are served; family members share the load. Guests can leave anytime; family members are committed to each other. Guests only see the living room; family members go into the kitchen to cook and wash dishes together. Paul says we are being built into God’s house, “in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord” (Ephesians 2:21).

After baptism you are no longer a guest of the church but a member of God’s household. This family has flaws, because everyone in it is still growing; but it was established by God, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone. Starting today, try seeing church through family eyes: greet people first, remember names, welcome newcomers. You were welcomed like that once; now it’s your turn to welcome others.
lessons.light: I don’t go to church—I am the church. Moving from guest to family means moving from being served to serving too; from consumer to member. It is a change of mindset and a sign of growth.
think: At church, are you more like a “guest” or “family”?
Which difference between guest and family touches you most?
What is the first thing you could do for God’s household?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you that I am no longer a stranger or foreigner but a member of your household. Help me move from guest to family and take part in your home with love. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Arrive ten minutes early this Sunday, greet three brothers or sisters, and ask their names.
lessons.quick: I’m not a guest at church—I’m part of God’s household.

lessons.title: The Body of Christ
text: For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ.
Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually.
lessons.hear:
Paul uses the body as a picture of the church: “For as the body is one and has many members, and all the members of the body, being many, are one body; so also is Christ” (1 Corinthians 12:12). Hands, feet, eyes and ears have different functions, yet belong to one body and need each other.

He continues: “Now you are the body of Christ, and members individually” (1 Corinthians 12:27). Every believer is part of Christ’s body; no one is unnecessary. Maybe you feel you have no gifts or nothing to contribute, but in a body, the least noticeable parts are often indispensable. When a little finger is hurt, the whole person feels it.

A member cut off from the body withers. Likewise, a Christian who stays away from the church community for a long time will find it hard to stay spiritually healthy. Not because church earns us something, but because we really are one body and need to supply and support one another. You need the church, and the church needs you.
lessons.light: Only the selfless can be one. Every member of the body works for the whole, not for itself. In the church it isn’t about who is more important; we all belong to Christ.
think: Which part of Christ’s body do you think you might be?
“The least noticeable parts are often indispensable”—do you believe it?
What do you need from the church? What can you supply?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, thank you for making me part of your body. I want to find my place in it, receive from other members and supply them too. Don’t let me be a lone believer anymore. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Send a brother or sister from church a message: “Thank you—I’m so glad we’re family.”
lessons.quick: You need the church, and the church needs you.

lessons.title: Don’t Stop Meeting Together
text: Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works,
not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching.
lessons.hear:
A glowing coal kept among other coals keeps burning brightly; take it out and set it aside, and it soon cools and turns black. A Christian’s life is the same: it needs other believers to stay on fire.

The writer of Hebrews says: “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching” (Hebrews 10:24-25). Gathering isn’t only listening to a sermon; it is spurring one another on and encouraging one another. You go to be built up, and to build up others.

Modern life is busy, and it’s easy to find reasons not to gather: too tired, bad weather, too much work, tension with someone. But “the custom of some”—making a habit of staying away—is dangerous. It starts with once or twice and slowly becomes a habit, until we drift away. Treat gathering like a family meal: part of life, not an activity for when you have spare time.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships: spiritual life stays warm in relationships. Gathering isn’t duty; it is building each other up in love. A coal near other coals keeps burning.
think: Have you ever slipped into the habit of dropping a good habit?
What reminder does the glowing coal give you?
When you gather, how can you “provoke” others to love?
lessons.speak: Lord, keep me from forsaking our assembling together. Let me stay in the fire like a coal, always burning. And use me in our gatherings to spur others to love and good works. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Put your Sunday service and home-group times into your calendar as weekly recurring events.
lessons.quick: A coal taken from the fire cools; so does a believer away from community.

lessons.title: Life in the Early Church
text: Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart,
praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved.
lessons.hear:
How did the early believers live? The Bible says: “Day by day, continuing steadfastly with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread at home, they took their food with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God and having favor with all the people. The Lord added to the assembly day by day those who were being saved” (Acts 2:46-47).

There are two places of gathering: “in the temple,” large public worship like today’s Sunday service; and “at home,” small household gatherings like today’s home groups. Both matter: large gatherings let us worship and hear the word together; small gatherings let us know one another, share life and care for each other.

Their life had a mark: “gladness and singleness of heart.” Not grudgingly keeping rules, but joyfully being together. The result was “favor with all the people,” and “the Lord added… day by day those who were being saved.” A loving community is itself the best testimony to the gospel. When people see Christians loving one another, they want to know: why are they like this?
lessons.light: Early church life was “life first, then relationships, then ministry”: first God’s life, then loving relationships, and the fruit of the gospel followed naturally. Building God’s order begins with a household like this.
think: Of the two kinds of gathering—“in the temple” and “at home”—which do you attend now?
Do you experience “gladness and singleness of heart” in gatherings?
Why does a loving community draw people?
lessons.speak: Father, in your house let me also have a glad and sincere heart—worshiping, eating and living with my brothers and sisters. Let our love be the best testimony. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: If you haven’t joined a home group yet, ask the person walking with you to arrange a visit this week. If you have, invite a group member for a meal.
lessons.quick: A community that loves one another is itself the gospel.

lessons.title: Commitment Is Love’s Response
text: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
lessons.hear:
Modern people are wary of “commitment,” because it means promises, giving and not being able to leave whenever we like. Yet every good relationship needs commitment: marriage, friendship—and faith too.

Paul says: “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). Notice “by the mercies of God.” Commitment isn’t because we are required or forced, but because we have seen God’s mercy—he gave himself completely to us, so we gladly give ourselves to him.

Committing to a church is one concrete expression of committing to God: gathering regularly, becoming a member, joining a home group, being willing to serve and give, and welcoming spiritual care and correction. This isn’t losing freedom but finding belonging. A tree planted in one place can put down roots and bear fruit; a tree constantly moved around struggles to grow.
lessons.light: Commitment responds to love, not to rules. Seeing God’s mercy, we gladly offer our bodies as living sacrifices. This is a concrete act of letting Jesus reign: my time, my body, my all belong to him.
think: What fears or hesitations do you have about “commitment”?
How does “by the mercies of God” as a motive change things for you?
Are you ready to commit to a church and become a member?
lessons.speak: Merciful God, you gave yourself completely to me; I want to give myself to you as a living sacrifice. I am willing to commit to your household, put down roots, grow and bear fruit. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Ask your church (or the person walking with you) about the membership process. If you are ready, sign up, and record this step on the Journey tab.
lessons.quick: Commitment isn’t losing freedom—it’s finding where you belong.

weeks.title: Home Group: A Spiritual Family
weeks.theme: The home group is the church’s basic unit of life, where we know, support and grow with one another in love.
group: How has home group been for you? What do you like most, and what is still unfamiliar?
Who in your home group has supported you?
How can you become a blessing in your home group?
weeks.guide: Help them move from “attending a home group” to “belonging to a home group.” Encourage them to share, pray for others and check in on one member. Explain “life first, then relationships, then ministry”: home group isn’t only Bible study but life connection. If there is friction, help them respond with humility and forgiveness. Also begin introducing 920 and 235: who around them is their “2”?
weeks.meet: This week, attend home group with the person walking with you. Afterward, talk: is there someone in the group you’d like to get to know or check on?
weeks.keyText: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.

lessons.title: Two Are Better Than One
text: Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor.
For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.
Again, if two lie together, then they have warmth; but how can one keep warm alone?
If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken.
lessons.hear:
Wise Solomon said: “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9-10).

People were made for relationship. Alone you can go fast; together you can go far. On the road of faith we will fall: faith grows weak, temptation comes, trouble at home, failure at work. Whether someone is there to lift you up makes a huge difference. Solomon concludes: “If a man prevails against one who is alone, two shall withstand him; and a threefold cord is not quickly broken” (Ecclesiastes 4:12).

A home group is such a threefold cord. There you can be known, cared for and prayed for, and you can know, care for and pray for others. Some Christians are afraid to be weak in front of others and always tough it out alone. But admitting you need help is humility, and sharing weakness in home group is often the beginning of healing.
lessons.light: People matter more than things; relationships matter more than possessions. The selfless aren’t afraid to let others see their weakness, and they gladly lift up a fallen companion. This is the “2” in 235: becoming spiritual companions with selfless people.
think: The last time you “fell,” did someone lift you up?
Do you find it easier to share weakness or to tough it out alone?
Who might be your “threefold cord”?
lessons.speak: Father, thank you for giving me spiritual family. Help me stop toughing it out alone, be willing to be known and supported in my home group, and support others too. Make us a threefold cord. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: In your home group or group chat, share one thing you need prayer for, and pray for one member’s need and tell them you did.
lessons.quick: Falling alone is dangerous; two can lift each other up.

lessons.title: From House to House
text: how I didn’t shrink from declaring to you anything that was profitable, teaching you publicly and from house to house,
lessons.hear:
Paul served in Ephesus for three years. Before leaving, he told the church elders that he had not held back anything helpful, “teaching you publicly and from house to house” (Acts 20:20). Paul didn’t only preach at big gatherings; he went house by house, teaching and walking with people.

Home is the most real place. At big gatherings we can dress neatly and smile; at home, around the table and in the living room, people find it easier to speak truthfully and be themselves. That is why home groups often meet in homes: eating, drinking tea, talking and praying together, lives connect naturally.

A home group isn’t a mini Sunday service but a spiritual family. Someone watches the children, someone brings snacks, someone leads songs, someone shares, someone cares. When you find your place in a home group, you discover that church isn’t only a place on Sunday but a family during the week.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the home group is where life and relationships connect most naturally. From house to house, faith moves from the pulpit into life, from knowledge into mutual love.
think: Why do people find it easier to be honest at home?
Could your home become a place for gathering?
What small role could you take on in your home group?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for bringing faith into our homes. Use our home group, so that around tables and in living rooms we know and love one another. Let my home also be a place that blesses others. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Take on one small task in your home group (bring snacks, send reminders, pray for everyone) and begin finding your place.
lessons.quick: Church isn’t only a place on Sunday—it’s a family during the week.

lessons.title: Love One Another
text: A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.
By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”
lessons.hear:
Before the Last Supper, Jesus bent down to wash his disciples’ feet, then said: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another. By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 13:34-35).

“Love one another” wasn’t new; the Old Testament said “love your neighbor as yourself.” What was new was the standard: “just as I have loved you.” How did Jesus love us? He washed feet—the lowliest task; he forgave the one who betrayed him; he gave his life for us. This is selfless love—not asking whether the other deserves it, but loving because we ourselves have been loved.

Jesus said the mark by which the world recognizes his disciples isn’t how much Bible we know or how many meetings we attend, but our love for one another. A home group with great Bible study but coldness and criticism loses its witness; a home group that may not explain doctrine well but truly cares for one another is the most beautiful witness.
lessons.light: Only the selfless can be one; loving one another is selflessness in practice. Pride against pride, both lose; humility bringing out humility, both win. In a home group, wash someone else’s feet first, and love begins to flow.
think: How has Jesus loved you? What moves you most?
In your home group or family, who is hardest for you to love?
How could you “wash someone’s feet”—a lowly act of love?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, as you have loved me, I want to love others. I admit it’s hard for me to love ___. Put your love in my heart so I can bend down to serve first. Let people recognize your disciples by our love. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Do a “foot-washing” act for a home-group member (or family member): a small task no one wants to do that would really help them.
lessons.quick: The world recognizes disciples by their love for one another.

lessons.title: Bear One Another’s Burdens
text: Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness, looking to yourself so that you also aren’t tempted.
Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (Galatians 6:2). Everyone carries burdens: illness, financial pressure, family problems, rebellious children, caring for aging parents. Some burdens are too heavy for one person; two or three carrying them together can keep going.

“Bearing one another’s burdens” is very concrete: sitting with a hospitalized member, helping with school runs, bringing a meal, lending money in an emergency, answering a late-night call. It includes spiritual burden-bearing too; Paul says just before, “Brothers, even if a man is caught in some fault, you who are spiritual must restore such a one in a spirit of gentleness” (Galatians 6:1). When a member falls, we don’t gossip; we restore gently.

To bear one another’s burdens, we must first know one another. Many people only share good news in home group and don’t dare voice their real burdens. That needs a safe, trusting, confidential environment. You can start with yourself: honestly share your need, and sincerely listen to others. When a home group becomes a place to set burdens down, it becomes a true spiritual family.
lessons.light: Self-denial is living for Jesus and others, not for self. Bearing one another’s burdens is self-denial in practice, and it is 920 practice: in every relationship, bearing the fruit of love through the selfless “0.”
think: What burden do you hope someone will carry with you right now?
Whose burden near you could you help carry?
Is your home group a safe place to tell the truth?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for carrying the heaviest burden for me. Help me let others share my burdens, and be willing to share theirs. Let me restore the fallen with gentleness. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Ask a home-group member (or friend): “What’s the heaviest thing you’re carrying lately? How can I help?” Then do one practical thing.
lessons.quick: What one can’t carry, two or three can.

lessons.title: Life, Then Relationships, Then Ministry
text: He went up into the mountain and called to himself those whom he wanted, and they went to him.
He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach
and to have authority to heal sicknesses and to cast out demons:
lessons.hear:
When Jesus chose the twelve disciples, the Bible records his purpose: “He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach and to have authority to heal sicknesses and to cast out demons” (Mark 3:14-15). Notice the order: first “that they might be with him,” then “send them out to preach.”

This is what 321 calls “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” Jesus didn’t first give his disciples a ministry manual; he first let them be with him, watching how he prayed, loved people and faced opposition. Three years of being with him shaped their lives; with that life came the ministry that later changed the world.

It’s the same in a home group: first life in Jesus, then relationships with one another, then serving together. Reverse the order—chase ministry while neglecting life and relationships—and we end up “hurting people for the sake of tasks” and “breaking relationships for the sake of things.” People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. This week we met the home group as a spiritual family. Next week we look at a family’s most natural expression: giving and serving together.
lessons.light: Life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. Don’t hurt people for the sake of tasks; don’t break relationships for the sake of things. This is the root order of building God’s order.
think: Why does “be with him” come before “send them out to preach”?
Have you seen people “hurt for the sake of tasks”?
In your life, is the order of life, relationships and ministry right?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, I want first to be with you often and let you shape my life; then build relationships with my brothers and sisters; and then serve together. Keep me from hurting people for the sake of tasks or breaking relationships for the sake of things. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Review this week’s time: how much went to “being with the Lord,” “building relationships,” and “doing tasks”? Make one adjustment.
lessons.quick: Life first, then relationships, then ministry.

weeks.title: Giving and Serving
weeks.theme: Everything belongs to God; we give gladly and serve with our gifts, serving others as Jesus did.
group: What concerns or questions do you have about “giving”?
What gifts do you think you might have?
Where could you begin a small act of service this week?
weeks.guide: New believers often have doubts about giving—some have even heard “churches only want money.” Explain the meaning of giving honestly (everything is God’s, a grateful response, supporting the work of God’s household), stress gladness without pressure, and share your own journey of learning to give. For serving, help them start small (welcoming, setting up chairs, bringing snacks, praying for people) and use the five questions of Spirit–Understanding–Life–Service–God to align their heart. Remind them: serving is life overflowing, not a stage to prove ourselves.
weeks.meet: This week, join a small act of service with the person walking with you (for example, Sunday welcome team or home-group prep), then talk about how it felt.
weeks.keyText: For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”

lessons.title: Everything Is God’s
text: Yours, LORD, is the greatness, the power, the glory, the victory, and the majesty! For all that is in the heavens and on the earth is yours. Yours is the kingdom, LORD, and you are exalted as head above all.
Both riches and honor come from you, and you rule over all! In your hand is power and might! It is in your hand to make great, and to give strength to all!
Now therefore, our God, we thank you and praise your glorious name.
But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own.
lessons.hear:
In his later years, King David prepared huge amounts of gold and silver to build the temple, and the people gave willingly too. David prayed before everyone a beautiful prayer: “But who am I, and what is my people, that we should be able to offer so willingly as this? For all things come from you, and we have given you of your own” (1 Chronicles 29:14).

These words change how we see money. We often think money is “mine,” and giving is sharing some of “mine” with God. But David says everything is God’s; we simply return to him part of what we received from him. Like a child who uses the allowance Dad gave him to buy Dad a birthday present—Dad is delighted not because of the price, but because of the child’s heart.

Understanding that “everything is God’s” frees us from two bondages: greed that won’t let go, and anxiety that fears there won’t be enough. We are managers of God’s resources, not owners. A manager’s job is to use the owner’s things according to the owner’s wishes—money, and also time, talents, body and our whole life.
lessons.light: Let Jesus receive all the glory, because everything is God’s. We are stewards, not owners—letting Jesus reign over money. Letting go of “mine” frees us from greed and anxiety.
think: Do you usually think of money as “mine” or “God’s”?
How does the child buying Dad a gift with Dad’s money make you feel?
With money, do you tend more toward greed or anxiety?
lessons.speak: Father, all things come from you; everything I have is your gift. Help me be a faithful steward—neither greedy nor anxious—gladly returning to you what I have received from you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: List three concrete ways God has provided for you this month (income, health, family…) and thank him for each.
lessons.quick: We only give God what we first received from him.

lessons.title: Cheerful Giving
text: Remember this: he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully.
Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver.
And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work.
lessons.hear:
Paul encouraged the Corinthian church to give to believers in need. He said: “Let each man give according as he has determined in his heart, not grudgingly or under compulsion, for God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). God values not the amount but the heart: cheerful, not forced.

Paul also states a spiritual principle: “he who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly. He who sows bountifully will also reap bountifully” (2 Corinthians 9:6). This isn’t an investment trick—“give a hundred and God returns a thousand.” It means generous people experience more of God’s provision and joy. He continues: “And God is able to make all grace abound to you, that you, always having all sufficiency in everything, may abound to every good work” (2 Corinthians 9:8).

Many churches encourage believers to learn the “tithe”—giving a tenth of their income to God as an exercise of gratitude and trust. New believers can start small and with a plan; what matters most is a cheerful heart. Giving is an exercise of faith: giving to God first declares, “I trust God as my provider,” not money.
lessons.light: Cheerful giving is selflessness in action: not clutching for ourselves, but giving for God’s kingdom. God loves a cheerful giver; the heart of giving matters more than the amount.
think: What concerns did you have about giving before?
“God loves a cheerful giver”—how can giving become “cheerful”?
Are you willing to begin learning to give with a plan?
lessons.speak: God, I want to learn to give cheerfully—not grudgingly, but out of gratitude and trust that you are my provider. Free me from the grip of money, and let me experience the joy of giving. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Talk with the person walking with you about giving, and set a plan to begin (an amount or percentage), starting with prayer.
lessons.quick: God values not the amount, but a cheerful heart.

lessons.title: Each According to the Gift Received
text: As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

If anyone speaks, let it be as it were the very words of God. If anyone serves, let it be as of the strength which God supplies, that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom belong the glory and the dominion forever and ever. Amen.
lessons.hear:
Peter says: “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms” (1 Peter 4:10). A “gift” is an ability God freely gives to build others up. Every believer has gifts, without exception—and gifts aren’t for showing off but for “serving one another.”

Gifts come in many forms: some teach, some care, some organize, some make music, some show hospitality, some make things with their hands, some excel in prayer, some in encouragement. Peter says those who speak should speak as God’s words, and those who serve should serve by the strength God supplies, “that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 4:11).

How do you discover your gifts? By serving. Many wait to know their gifts before serving, but often it works the other way: begin serving, and discover where you find the most joy, bless people most, and are often affirmed by others. Start with small things, and ask the person walking with you or your home group: “What gifts do you think I have?”
lessons.light: A gift isn’t my achievement but God’s entrustment; I am a steward, not an owner. The purpose of serving is that God be glorified through Jesus Christ in all things—not that I be glorified.
think: What gifts do you think you might have?
In what area do others often affirm you?
What small service could you start with, to discover your gifts along the way?
lessons.speak: God, thank you for giving me gifts. I don’t yet know clearly what they are, but I’m willing to begin serving and discover them along the way. Use me, so that you are glorified through Jesus Christ in all things. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Ask three brothers or sisters who know you: “Where do you think I bless people most?” Write down their answers.
lessons.quick: Gifts are God’s entrustment, for serving one another.

lessons.title: The Son of Man Came to Serve
text: Jesus summoned them and said to them, “You know that they who are recognized as rulers over the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.
But it shall not be so among you, but whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant.
Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all.
For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.”
lessons.hear:
The disciples once argued about who was greatest; James and John even privately asked Jesus to let them sit at his right and left in the future. When the others heard, they were angry. Jesus called them together and said: “Whoever wants to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever of you wants to become first among you shall be bondservant of all” (Mark 10:43-44).

Then Jesus gave the mission statement of his life: “For the Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many” (Mark 10:45). The world’s logic says: the greater you are, the more people serve you. Jesus’ kingdom is the opposite: the greater you are, the more you serve others.

Serving isn’t climbing to a higher position, or being seen and praised. True service is doing a servant’s work out of love, as Jesus did. Maybe setting up chairs, washing dishes, sitting with a lonely elder, driving a child somewhere—small in people’s eyes, great in God’s. When you serve like this, you aren’t only working for Jesus; you are living out Jesus.
lessons.light: Pride competes to be great; humility gladly serves. The way of service: let Jesus live and reign in me, and serve by his authority and power; everything is God’s grace—give thanks in all things and give the glory to Jesus.
think: Do you have a heart that competes to be great and wants to be seen?
How is “the greater you are, the more you serve” different from the world’s logic?
What “servant’s task” could you do?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you came not to be served but to serve, even giving your life. Take away my heart that competes to be great, and let me gladly be a servant, living out who you are. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: At church or at home, do one act of service no one will see and no one needs to thank you for.
lessons.quick: In God’s kingdom, the greater you are, the more you serve.

lessons.title: The Way of Service: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God
text: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:23-24). The one we serve is the Lord, not people; the motive comes from the heart, not from wanting to perform.

321 sums up the heart of service in five words. Spirit—the Holy Spirit is my guide: before serving, seek the Spirit’s leading and prompting. Understanding—the Bible is my standard: understand and obey the truth of Scripture. Life—Jesus is my example: cultivate and live out the life of Jesus. Service—let Jesus reign: let Jesus live and reign in me, and serve by his authority and power. God—let Jesus receive all the glory: everything is what God has done and accomplished in Jesus, all grace; give thanks in everything and give the glory to Jesus.

Before each act of service, align your heart with five questions: Have I sought the Spirit’s leading? Am I following Scripture? Am I living like Jesus? Is Jesus reigning, or am I in charge? Who gets the glory? This week we learned about giving and serving. In the final week we take the most important step: becoming a spiritual parent and walking with the next person.
lessons.light: The way of service: Spirit—the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding—the Bible is my standard; Life—Jesus is my example; Service—let Jesus reign; God—let Jesus receive all the glory.
think: How does “as for the Lord and not for men” change your attitude in serving?
Of the five words, which do you most need to strengthen?
When serving, whose approval have you wanted?
lessons.speak: Lord Christ, it is you I serve. Holy Spirit, lead me; let me follow your word, live out your life, let you reign in me, and give all the glory to you. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Before your next act of service, pray through the five questions of Spirit–Understanding–Life–Service–God, and afterward reflect on what was different.
lessons.quick: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God: work heartily, as for the Lord.

weeks.title: Becoming a Spiritual Parent
weeks.theme: Those who were accompanied go on to accompany others; through 920 and 235 we build God’s order in relationships.
group: Looking back over these 24 weeks, what are you most grateful for?
Who comes to mind as someone God wants you to walk with?
Are you ready to begin the journey of becoming a spiritual parent?
weeks.guide: This is graduation week—and handing-on week. Look back over the journey together and thank God for their growth. Invite them to begin as a spiritual parent: they don’t need to be very mature, only one step ahead of the other person. Help them add the first person they want to walk with on the Companion tab, and agree on your relationship going forward (from spiritual parent and child to spiritual companions and co-workers). Finally, pray together for the person they will walk with, and bless and send them.
weeks.meet: This week, look back over the whole journey with the person walking with you, and pray together for the person you will walk with next.
weeks.keyText: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.

lessons.title: Entrust to Faithful People
text: The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also.
lessons.hear:
Near the end of his life, Paul wrote to his spiritual son Timothy: “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men who will be able to teach others also” (2 Timothy 2:2). This verse contains four generations: Paul, Timothy, faithful people, and others. Faith is passed on like this, generation after generation.

You know Jesus today because someone walked with you; the one who walked with you was once walked with by someone else. It’s a very long relay race, starting with Jesus and his disciples, passed on for two thousand years, and now into your hands. You are invited to take the baton and pass what you have received to the next person.

You may think, “I’ve only just believed—who could I walk with?” But becoming a spiritual parent doesn’t require being perfect or very knowledgeable—only being one step ahead. A toddler who has just learned to walk can hold a younger sibling’s hand. Your struggles, questions, family opposition and fears about baptism are exactly what the next seeker needs someone to walk through with them.
lessons.light: Those who were accompanied go on to accompany others. This is how God’s order is built: not by one great person, but by generation after generation of selfless companionship. The “3” in 235 is building spiritual parent–child relationships.
think: On your journey to faith, who walked with you?
How does “only one step ahead” give you courage?
Who is the person who comes to mind?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for walking with me through ___ so that I came to know you. I want to take the baton too and pass on what I have received. Show me the one you want me to walk with. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: On the Companion tab, add the first person you want to walk with (a family member, friend or coworker), and pray for them.
lessons.quick: You only need to be one step ahead to walk with someone.

lessons.title: A Spiritual Parent’s Heart
text: But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children.
Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us.
lessons.hear:
Paul describes how he walked with the Thessalonian believers: “But we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishes her own children. Even so, affectionately longing for you, we were well pleased to impart to you not the Good News of God only, but also our own souls, because you had become very dear to us” (1 Thessalonians 2:7-8).

Paul compares himself to a mother, and then later says “as a father does his own children” (1 Thessalonians 2:11), exhorting, comforting and urging them. A spiritual parent’s heart is a parent’s heart: gentle, patient, willing to give, caring more about the child’s growth than their own convenience.

Paul says he was glad to share not only the gospel but “our own souls.” Walking with someone isn’t only explaining doctrine or leading Bible study; it is sharing your life: eating together, listening, showing up when they need you, praying for them, not giving up when they stumble. This is how you were walked with, and now you can walk with others. It can be tiring, but when you see someone move from doubt to faith, from wounded to healed, from baptism to walking with others too, the joy is beyond compare.
lessons.light: A spiritual parent’s heart is a selfless heart: giving not only the gospel but our own lives. Walking with someone isn’t managing or controlling, but loving gently, patiently and self-givingly, like a parent.
think: In what way was the person who walked with you most like “a nursing mother”?
“Not only the gospel, but our own lives”—are you ready?
What worries you most about being a spiritual parent?
lessons.speak: Father, give me a spiritual parent’s heart: gentle, patient and willing to give. Not only giving the gospel, but sharing my life. Use me to bless others. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Read the “Five Principles of Walking With Someone” on the Companion tab, and invite the person you want to walk with for coffee—listen to their story first.
lessons.quick: A spiritual parent gives not only the gospel but their life.

lessons.title: 920: Bearing Fruit in Relationships
text: I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.
“In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples.
lessons.hear:
Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). And: “In this my Father is glorified, that you bear much fruit; and so you will be my disciples” (John 15:8).

321 calls the practice of bearing fruit “920”: everyone connected to you is your “2”; in every relationship, practicing the selfless “0” bears the nine fruits of the Spirit, the “9”—the life of Christ. Your spouse, children, parents, coworkers, neighbors, home-group members—even the person who gives you headaches—are your “2.”

Being a spiritual parent is 920 practice too. Walking with a seeker, you will need patience (they keep asking the same question), gentleness (they say something offensive), faithfulness (you promised to walk with them) and self-control (don’t keep talking—listen more). These fruits aren’t squeezed out by you; they grow naturally as you remain in Jesus. Apart from him we can do nothing; remaining in him, we bear much fruit.
lessons.light: 920: everyone connected to us is our “2”; practice living the selfless “0”; bear the “9” fruits of the Spirit—the life of Christ. Only by remaining on the vine can we bear much fruit in relationships.
think: Who are the five most important “2”s in your life?
In which relationship do you most need to practice the “0” (selflessness)?
When walking with someone, which fruit of the Spirit will you need most?
lessons.speak: Lord Jesus, you are the vine and I am a branch. Help me remain in you, practice selflessness in every relationship, and bear the fruit of the Spirit, so the Father is glorified. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: On the Companion tab’s 920 circle, add the five most important people in your life. This week, pray for and check in on each of them once.
lessons.quick: Each relationship is a 2; practice the selfless 0; bear the Spirit’s 9.

lessons.title: 235: Companions, Parents, Co-workers
text: He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers;
for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ,
until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ,
lessons.hear:
Paul says: “He gave some to be apostles; and some, prophets; and some, evangelists; and some, shepherds and teachers; for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ, until we all attain to the unity of the faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a full grown man, to the measure of the stature of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4:11-13). God sets different ministries in the church so that every believer grows and joins in serving.

321 uses “235” to describe how spiritual relationships develop: “2”—becoming spiritual companions with selfless people who aren’t stuck in their problems, supporting each other; “3”—building spiritual parent–child relationships, passing faith from generation to generation; “5”—becoming spiritual co-workers, a team of the fivefold ministries (apostle, prophet, evangelist, shepherd, teacher) building God’s kingdom together.

Your 24-week journey began as a “child” being walked with. Next, you can become spiritual companions with the one who walked with you, and begin to be someone else’s spiritual parent. One day, you and many others can become spiritual co-workers, building God’s domain on earth together. This is building God’s order: not one person’s ministry, but a group of selfless people letting Jesus reign together in relationship.
lessons.light: 235: develop “2” spiritual companionship with selfless people, build “3” spiritual parent–child relationships, and become a “5” team of spiritual co-workers in the fivefold ministries. Only the selfless can build God’s order; only the selfless can build God’s kingdom.
think: Do you have a “2” spiritual companion now? Who?
In “3” relationships, are you a child, a parent, or both?
Are you willing one day to be part of a “5” team of spiritual co-workers?
lessons.speak: Lord, thank you for letting me grow in relationships. Give me spiritual companions, make me a spiritual parent to others, and one day let me become a spiritual co-worker with my brothers and sisters, building your kingdom together. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: On the Companion tab’s 235 section, write the names of your spiritual companion, your spiritual parent, and the spiritual child you want to walk with.
lessons.quick: Companions support, parents pass on, co-workers build—that’s 235.

lessons.title: Your Kingdom Come
text: Pray like this: “‘Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
lessons.hear:
This is the last lesson of the 24 weeks. We began with the empty place in the human heart and walked through God’s existence, who Jesus is, the cross and resurrection, grace and our response, prayer and Bible reading, baptism and commitment to the church, all the way to beginning as a spiritual parent today. Every step of the way has been God’s grace.

Finally, we return to the prayer Jesus taught us: “Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:9-10). One purpose of 321 is “building God’s order”—that is, seeing the Lord’s Prayer fulfilled on earth: people honoring God’s name as holy, God’s kingdom coming, God’s will done on earth as in heaven, and the kingdom, power and glory all belonging to God.

This isn’t a distant dream. It starts with you, with your home, with the person you walk with. When one person moves from self-centered to selfless and lets Jesus reign within, God’s kingdom comes a little more right there. Change starts with me. May you let Jesus reign all your life and give him all the glory; may you be an overcomer and one day sit with Christ on his throne in God’s kingdom. Your journey isn’t over; it is a new beginning.
lessons.light: Three foundations: Jesus is my example, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Two cores: let Jesus reign, let Jesus receive all the glory. One purpose: build God’s order. Change starts with me.
think: Looking back over the 24 weeks, what is the biggest change in your life?
“Your Kingdom come”—what might that look like, starting with you?
How do you want to keep growing over the next year?
lessons.speak: Our Father in heaven, may your name be kept holy. Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven. Lord, start with me, with my home, with the person I walk with. Let Jesus reign in me, and let all the glory be yours. In the name of the Lord Jesus I pray, Amen.
lessons.do: Write a letter to the person who walked with you, thanking them; also write your spiritual goals for the coming year. Then begin walking with the next person.
lessons.quick: Your Kingdom come—starting with me.
